911.title: The Geonim
911.hook: heads of the Babylonian academies answer questions from Jews across the world
911.howItsDone: Jews today still turn to the Geonim's surviving letters and rulings as early witnesses to how the Talmud was read, and historians study the Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon for its account of the Mishnah and Talmud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Babylonian Talmud: a first page that asks where the teacher is standing, and Rav Ashi and Ravina as the end. Your line was the talmud sealed. Did you ask where a rule comes from? Day nine hundred eleven.

A community in Kairouan, in North Africa, has a question it can't settle. Not about a holiday or a meal. A history question: how was the Mishnah written? And the Talmud, how did it come together? Who did what, and in what order? So Rabbi Jacob ben Nissim, a teacher there, writes a letter and send it a very long way east, to the head of the academy at Pumbedita. And an answer comes back. The answer is long, careful, and so useful that people are still reading it. We're starting a new stretch of the story today: Babylon, the Islamic world, and the first Ashkenazim.
screen: `A QUESTION IN KAIROUAN.` → `HOW WAS THE MISHNAH WRITTEN?` → `A LETTER EAST TO PUMBEDITA.`

segments.voice: After the Talmud was sealed, the academies of Sura and Pumbedita went on. Their heads came to carry a title: Gaon, and in the plural, Geonim. The title is usually explained as short for the head of the academy that is the pride of Jacob. That phrase comes from a psalm, which in the 1917 Jewish translation reads "The pride of Jacob whom He loveth." In everyday Hebrew, gaon came to mean a genius. But here it is a job title, and the job was to teach, and to answer. Jewish communities were spread across a huge distance. The Talmud was the shared text, but it is long and hard, and real life keeps producing cases it never quite covered. So letters traveled to the Geonim. The Geonim read the question, studied it, and wrote back. The letter from Kairouan reached Rav Sherira Gaon, head of Pumbedita. His reply, known as the Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon, walks through how the Mishnah and the Talmud took shape, teacher by teacher. Here is the picture to hold. A text sealed in one place, and a web of letters spreading it to many others. Letters across the world. A question written in one city, an answer written in another, and the conversation of the academies reaching people who had never seen them.
screen: `GAON: HEAD OF THE ACADEMY.` · `THE PRIDE OF JACOB.` · `THE LETTER OF RAV SHERIRA GAON.` · then, large: `LETTERS ACROSS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to write down one question. Sit, and let the first breaths settle. Then let a real question come to mind, not a quiz question, a question you actually carry. About your tradition, your family's story, a text you never understood, a choice in front of you. Don't answer it. Just find the words for it, the way the people of Kairouan found theirs. Make it clear enough that someone far away could understand it. After the bell, write it down somewhere you'll see it again. If you pray, you can bring that question to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Gaon. The title of the heads of the Babylonian academies, the Geonim, who answered questions sent from far away. Today's word.
Your line: letters across the world. Today, send one real message to someone far away, a question or a thank you, written with care. Day nine hundred eleven.

912.title: Questions and answers
912.hook: responsa, rulings sent by letter, a form of Jewish law that continues today
912.howItsDone: Jews with a question of Jewish law often ask a rabbi, and rabbis today still write formal teshuvot, citing the Talmud and earlier responsa, on new questions as they arise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Geonim, and a question from Kairouan answered by Rav Sherira Gaon. Your line was letters across the world. Did you send one? Today, the shape those letters took. Day nine hundred twelve.

A prayer book that began as a reply. Tradition says a community in Spain wrote to Rav Amram, a Gaon of Sura, asking how the prayers of the year should be said. He wrote back with the order of the prayers, set out with their rules. That answer, known as the Order of Rav Amram, is remembered as one of the early written orders of Jewish prayer. Look at the shape of it. Someone far away didn't know. They asked. Someone else took the question seriously and answered in full. Today's word is the name for that shape, and it's a word that already means something else in Hebrew.
screen: `A COMMUNITY IN SPAIN ASKS.` → `RAV AMRAM WRITES BACK.` → `A PRAYER BOOK BEGINS AS A REPLY.`

segments.voice: Teshuvot means answers. A single one is a teshuvah. The word is often heard as return, or repentance, the turning back to God of the High Holy Days. But the same Hebrew word also means a reply, a word that turns back to the one who asked. The Bible uses it that way. In the book of Job, Job tells his friends, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "as for your answers, there remaineth only faithlessness." The Hebrew word for answers there is the plural of teshuvah. In Jewish law, the full name of this form is she'elot u-teshuvot, questions and answers. In English it's called responsa. The shape is simple. At the top, the question, copied out: who is asking, what happened, what they need to know. Then the answer: the sources, the reasoning, and the ruling. The answer is written to a real person with a real problem, not to a textbook. That's what makes responsa precious to historians, too. Tucked into the questions is ordinary life: a business deal gone wrong, a marriage, a quarrel between neighbors. And the form never stopped. Rabbis still write teshuvot today, about things no Gaon could have pictured. A new question comes. Someone asks. Someone answers, citing the Talmud, the Geonim, and everyone in between. Ask and answer.
screen: `TESHUVAH: RETURN, AND REPLY.` · `IN YOUR ANSWERS, IN JOB.` · then, large: `QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS.` · `THE FORM NEVER STOPPED.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to ask someone a real question. Sit for a moment first. Yesterday you wrote down a question you carry. Now think of a person who might help with it, or with any question you've been holding back: an older relative, a teacher, a friend who knows more than you about something. Picture asking them. Notice what makes it hard: pride, shyness, not wanting to bother anyone. A teshuvah only exists because someone was willing to ask. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to ask. When the bell ends, decide when you'll ask them. The bell holds the time.
Teshuvot. Answers: the written replies of Jewish law, question at the top, answer below. The same word as teshuvah, return. Today's word.
Your line: ask and answer. Today, ask one real question, and when someone asks you one, answer it fully, with your reasons. Day nine hundred twelve.

913.title: Saadia Gaon
913.hook: a Gaon translates the Torah into Arabic and writes on faith and reason
913.howItsDone: Saadia's Arabic translation of the Torah is still read in some Yemenite Jewish communities alongside the Hebrew, and his Book of Beliefs and Opinions is studied in courses on Jewish thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teshuvot, the answers that cross the world by letter, and a prayer book that began as a reply. Your line was ask and answer. What did you ask? Today, a Gaon who took on questions about faith itself. Day nine hundred thirteen.

Believers whose belief is clouded. Doubters who are proud of doubting. And thoughtful people sinking, as he puts it, in a sea of confusion, with no one to pull them out. That is what one author sees when he looks around, and it worries him enough to write. Not a sermon. An argument, step by step, using reason, about what can be known and how. The author is Saadia, head of the academy at Sura. He's a Gaon, like the ones we met this week. But the questions he takes on aren't about one case of law. They're about whether faith and thinking can stand on the same ground.
screen: `A WORRIED AUTHOR.` → `PEOPLE SINKING IN CONFUSION.` → `SAADIA, GAON OF SURA.`

segments.voice: Saadia did two big things. First, he translated the Torah into Arabic, the everyday language of the Jews around him, and it has come down to us in Hebrew letters. It's often called his Tafsir, an Arabic word for explanation, because his translation explains as it goes. Second, he wrote the book from the hook, known in English as The Book of Beliefs and Opinions. In it he lays out how a person comes to know things: what the senses observe, what reason grasps, what you can necessarily infer, and reliable tradition, which for him includes the Torah. Here's his bold claim. Faith and reason don't compete. Rightly used, they lead to the same truth. Then he asks the obvious question back. If reason can reach it, why does anyone need revelation? His answer, in plain words: because thinking things through takes a long time, and some people never get there. Revelation gives the truth to everyone at once, the young and the busy included. Reason lets you understand it, test it, and defend it when someone challenges you. That's today's line: faith and reason. Not one instead of the other. Saadia's translation brought the Torah into the language of the street. His philosophy brought the street's hardest questions into the Torah.
screen: `THE TORAH IN ARABIC.` · `THE BOOK OF BELIEFS AND OPINIONS.` · then, large: `FAITH AND REASON, ONE TRUTH.` · `WHY REVELATION? IT REACHES EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to put one verse into your own words, the way a translator does. Here's the verse, from the Psalms, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, And a light unto my path." Sit, and say it slowly in your head. Then ask: how would I say this to someone who has never heard it, in the words I actually use? Try one version. Try another. Notice what gets lost and what gets clearer each time. A translation is an answer to the question, what does this mean? If you pray, you can end by saying the verse as it is written. The bell holds the time.
Saadia Gaon. Head of the academy at Sura, who translated the Torah into Arabic and wrote that faith and reason lead to one truth. Today's word.
Your line: faith and reason. Today, when something you value is questioned, look for the reason behind it, and put it into your own plain words. Day nine hundred thirteen.

914.title: Jews in the Islamic world
914.hook: Baghdad, Cairo, Kairouan: long periods of flourishing, and times of hardship
914.howItsDone: Jewish communities with roots in North Africa, the Middle East and Yemen keep traditions, melodies and words from centuries of life in Arabic-speaking lands, and Judeo-Arabic texts are still studied.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saadia Gaon, who put the Torah into Arabic and argued that faith and reason lead to one truth. Your line was faith and reason. Did you find the words for something you value? Day nine hundred fourteen.

Kitab. It's the Arabic word for a book. Saadia's great work of philosophy has it in its Arabic title. And it shows up in a phrase the Qur'an uses for Jews and Christians: ahl al-kitab, the people of the book, or as one old translation puts it, the People of the Scripture. In the copies of Saadia's book that came down to us, kitab is spelled in Hebrew letters. Arabic words, Hebrew script. That way of writing has a name, Judeo-Arabic, and it's a small window into a very big world. For centuries, from Baghdad to Cairo to Kairouan, Jewish life unfolded in lands ruled by Muslims, and in Arabic.
screen: `KITAB: A BOOK.` → `PEOPLE OF THE BOOK.` → `ARABIC WORDS, HEBREW LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The academies we've been following, Sura and Pumbedita, came to sit in a world governed by Muslim rulers, whose capital was Baghdad. Under Islamic law, Jews and Christians were usually treated as protected peoples, called dhimmi. They could keep their faith, their courts and their houses of worship. They also paid a special tax and lived under limits. How those limits felt depended a great deal on who was in power. There were long stretches of flourishing. Jews worked as merchants, doctors, scholars and officials. They wrote poetry, philosophy and Bible commentary in Arabic, and their letters crossed seas because trade routes did. Jewish thinkers read Muslim philosophers and argued with them; ideas moved in both directions. That's the world Saadia wrote from. There were also hard times. In Cairo, for a time, a caliph ordered synagogues and churches torn down, before the policy was reversed. Some rulers enforced humiliating rules. Communities sometimes faced violence, and some had to flee. Both of these are true, and the honest history keeps both. Neither the story of perfect harmony nor the story of constant persecution fits what the records show. So today's line is simple and exact: jews among muslims. Neighbors, business partners, rivals, sometimes victims, sometimes friends, living the long middle of history side by side, and writing it down in Arabic in Hebrew letters.
screen: `PROTECTED, AND LIMITED.` · `LONG STRETCHES OF FLOURISHING.` · `AND TIMES OF HARDSHIP.` · then, large: `BOTH ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to learn one Judeo-Arabic word: kitab, a book. It can be spelled in Arabic letters, and also in Hebrew ones, the way Saadia's book spells it. Sit and say it quietly a few times. Kitab. Then let it open a picture: a woman in Kairouan, writing to her brother in Arabic, in Hebrew letters, about a wedding, a sick child, the price of bread. Two languages in one line. Hold that picture without deciding what it means. Just let it be a real life. If you pray, you can remember the people of that world. The bell holds the time.
Dhimmi. The status of Jews and Christians as protected peoples under Islamic law, free to keep their faith but taxed and limited. Today's word.
Your line: jews among muslims. Today, when you hear a simple story about any two peoples, all good or all bad, ask what the longer story might hold. Day nine hundred fourteen.

915.title: The Cairo Geniza
915.hook: a storeroom where worn writings were kept, holding centuries of daily life
915.howItsDone: Synagogues and Jewish homes set aside worn prayer books, Bibles and other pages with God's name, and communities later bury them in a Jewish cemetery rather than throwing them away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jews in the Islamic world: flourishing and hardship, and kitab, a book, in Hebrew letters. Your line was jews among muslims. Did you look for the longer story? Today, a room where that story was kept. Day nine hundred fifteen.

A shopping list. A child's alphabet practice, the letters wobbling across the page. A marriage contract. A merchant's letter complaining about a late ship. A page of poetry. A page of the Torah, worn soft. All of it in one dark room high in the wall of a synagogue in old Cairo, the Ben Ezra synagogue. Nobody meant it as an archive. People put papers there for one reason: they had God's name on them, or holy words, or Hebrew letters, and you don't throw that in the trash. So for centuries, the paper piled up. Today's word is the name for that room.
screen: `A SHOPPING LIST, A CHILD'S ALPHABET.` → `A ROOM IN A CAIRO SYNAGOGUE.` → `YOU DON'T THROW IT IN THE TRASH.`

segments.voice: A geniza is a storeroom for worn-out holy writings. The idea is already in the Mishnah. In tractate Shabbat it says holy writings may be rescued from a fire, and that those which can't be read from are to be stored away. The Hebrew for that storing away is the same word: geniza. The custom grows from respect. A book with God's name in it is not just paper. So when a prayer book falls apart or a Torah scroll can no longer be read, it isn't thrown away. It's stored, and in time it may be buried, the way a person is. In Cairo, the pages stayed in the room, and the dry air seems to have kept them. And because people there seem to have put almost anything with Hebrew letters inside, the room ended up holding ordinary life: business letters, court records, recipes, prescriptions, love poems, and the handwriting of children learning to read. When scholars finally carried the papers out and began to read them, a world came back. Merchants trading across seas. Women in court over property. Families writing to sons far away. Here is today's line, and it's the reason any of this survived: nothing holy thrown away. A habit of respect for words became, without anyone planning it, a memory for a whole community.
screen: `A STOREROOM FOR WORN HOLY WRITINGS.` · `THE MISHNAH: STORE THEM AWAY.` · `THE ROOM HELD ORDINARY LIFE.` · then, large: `NOTHING HOLY THROWN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to keep one old letter. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind the papers in your life that carry someone: a card in a drawer, a note in a parent's handwriting, a message on your phone from someone who's gone, a child's drawing. Pick one. You don't need to get up yet. Just hold it in your mind and ask why you've kept it, or why you might. Ordinary words become precious when someone wrote them. After the bell, find it, and put it somewhere safe. If you pray, you can remember the person whose hand is on it. The bell holds the time.
Geniza. A storeroom for worn holy writings that aren't thrown away. In Cairo, one geniza kept centuries of daily life. Today's word.
Your line: nothing holy thrown away. Today, before you delete or throw out something with someone's words on it, pause, and ask if it should be kept. Day nine hundred fifteen.

916.title: The Karaites
916.hook: a movement that rejected the oral law and was argued with for centuries
916.howItsDone: Karaite communities still keep their own calendar, prayers and readings of the Torah, while Rabbanite Jews light Sabbath candles before sunset on Friday and let them burn into the evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cairo Geniza, a room that kept a world because nothing holy was thrown away. Your line was nothing holy thrown away. What did you keep? Today, a disagreement you could find in those very papers. Day nine hundred sixteen.

Friday evening, just before the Sabbath. In one Jewish home, the candles are lit, and they'll burn through the evening, giving light to the meal. In another Jewish home, a Karaite home of an earlier age, the lamps go out before the Sabbath begins, and the family keeps the holy day in the dark. Both homes read the same verse of the Torah. In the 1917 Jewish translation: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." Same verse. Both families Jewish. Two very different Friday nights. The difference comes down to one question: is the written Torah enough on its own?
screen: `FRIDAY EVENING, TWO HOMES.` → `CANDLES BURNING, OR THE DARK.` → `IS THE WRITTEN TORAH ENOUGH?`

segments.voice: The Karaites are Jews who hold that the written Torah, the scripture itself, is the authority, and who do not accept the oral law of the Mishnah and Talmud as binding. Their name is usually explained from mikra, a Hebrew word for scripture, the text that is read. Tradition names Anan ben David as an early leader of the movement in Babylonia, and it grew in the lands we met this week. Back to the verse. The rabbinic tradition, the Rabbanites, reads it with the oral law: you may not kindle a fire on the Sabbath, but a light lit beforehand may keep burning. So, Sabbath candles. Karaite teachers, reading the verse on its own, took it to mean no fire may burn in the home on the Sabbath, even one lit before; Karaite practice today varies. Both sides were reading closely. They just started from different places. And they argued, for centuries. Saadia Gaon wrote against Karaite views, and Karaite scholars wrote back. The argument made both sides read harder. If you rely on scripture alone, you need to know its Hebrew exactly. If you defend the oral law, you have to show how it fits the written words. The book of Proverbs says, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "Iron sharpeneth iron." The Talmud applies that verse to scholars who sharpen each other in study. That's today's line: argument sharpens. Karaite communities still exist today, keeping their own way.
screen: `SCRIPTURE ALONE.` · `KINDLE NO FIRE: TWO READINGS.` · `SAADIA WROTE; KARAITES WROTE BACK.` · then, large: `IRON SHARPENETH IRON.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to understand one group you disagree with. Sit, and slow your breath. Bring to mind a group whose way of doing things is different from yours, in faith, politics, family habits, anything. Now try the Karaite and Rabbanite exercise. What text, what value, or what experience do they start from? Then find one thing they are trying to protect, something you might care about too. You don't have to agree. Just see where they're standing. Notice if your own view gets clearer, too. If you pray, you can ask for a fair mind. The bell holds the time.
The Karaites. Jews who hold to the written Torah as the authority, without the oral law, and who argued with the rabbis for centuries. Today's word.
Your line: argument sharpens. Today, in one disagreement, ask the other person where they start from, before you answer. Day nine hundred sixteen.

917.title: Italy and Byzantium
917.hook: Jews have lived in Rome since before the Temple fell
917.howItsDone: Roman Jews and Romaniote Jews keep their own synagogue customs and prayer traditions, distinct from both Ashkenazi and Sephardi rites, and some still gather in historic synagogues in Rome and in Greece.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Karaites: a movement that set the oral law aside, and the rabbis who argued back. Your line was argument sharpens. Did a disagreement sharpen something in you? Today we leave Babylon and head west, to a very old address. Day nine hundred seventeen.

In the Roman Forum stands a stone arch built for a general named Titus. Walk under it and look up at the inside wall. Carved soldiers are carrying a great lampstand on poles, the Temple menorah, out of a city they have just burned. It is a victory picture, made by the winners. Some Roman Jews keep a custom of not walking under that arch at all. And here is the strange part. Their community was in Rome before the arch went up, and it is still there now that the empire that built it is gone. Today, the old Jewish communities of Italy and Byzantium: people who stayed, generation after generation, in the same streets.
screen: `AN ARCH FOR TITUS.` → `A MENORAH CARRIED AWAY.` → `THE COMMUNITY THAT STAYED.`

segments.voice: Start with the oldest written traces. The first book of Maccabees tells how Judah Maccabee sent envoys to Rome to make a treaty of friendship. That is a story from before the Temple fell, and tradition in Rome's Jewish community points back to ties like it. Then the New Testament gives two small snapshots. The book of Acts mentions a couple who had to leave the city, in the King James words, "because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome." And later, when Paul reaches Rome, Acts says he "called the chief of the Jews together." So by then there were Jewish leaders in the city to call. Even in stories about someone else, a Jewish community is already living there. Now turn east. When the Roman Empire split, its eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, is what historians call Byzantium. Greek-speaking Jews lived across its towns, in Greece, in the islands, in southern Italy, which Byzantium ruled for a long stretch. Their descendants are sometimes called Romaniote Jews, and they kept their own prayer customs and poems. From southern Italy comes a family chronicle in Hebrew, the Scroll of Ahimaaz, where a writer traces his ancestors through generations of teachers, poets and community leaders, with miracle stories woven in. History and family memory in one scroll. Life under Byzantine rule was not easy. The same scroll remembers an emperor who pressed Jews to convert, and times of hardship. But the communities held. And here is the thread that matters for tomorrow: teachers and families from Italy carried learning north, over the Alps. An old community is not just old. It is a place that keeps handing things on.
